stem: A search feature builds SQL queries by concatenating user input, exposing it to SQL injection. What is the BEST fix?

options.text: Use parameterized queries/prepared statements plus input validation
options.rationale: Parameterized queries separate code from data so input cannot alter the query structure, and input validation adds defense in depth — the standard SQL injection fix.

options.text: Concatenate the input more carefully with quotes
options.rationale: String concatenation, even with quoting, remains vulnerable; parameterization is required.

options.text: Hide the search box from most users
options.rationale: Hiding the UI does not remove the injectable endpoint.

options.text: Increase the database server's memory
options.rationale: Hardware resources do not prevent injection.

stem: A comment field displays user-supplied text back on the page, allowing scripts to execute in other users' browsers (XSS). Which control is the BEST primary defense?

options.text: Output encoding/escaping of user content (with input validation)
options.rationale: Encoding output so data cannot be interpreted as executable script is the primary defense against cross-site scripting.

options.text: Making the comment font larger
options.rationale: Font size has no security effect on XSS.

options.text: Storing comments in a faster database
options.rationale: Storage speed does not prevent script execution in browsers.

options.text: Disabling the site's logging
options.rationale: Disabling logging reduces detection and does nothing to prevent XSS.

stem: An app 'protects' an admin action by hiding the button in the UI, but the endpoint performs no authorization check. Why is this MOST inadequate?

options.text: Client-side controls are bypassable; authorization must be enforced server-side
options.rationale: Attackers can call the endpoint directly regardless of the UI, so access control must be enforced on the server — this is broken access control otherwise.

options.text: Because the button color is wrong
options.rationale: Button appearance is irrelevant to the access-control flaw.

options.text: Because hiding buttons is fully sufficient security
options.rationale: Hiding UI elements does not stop direct requests; it is not sufficient.

options.text: Because the server is too fast
options.rationale: Server speed is unrelated to the missing authorization check.

stem: For validating user input, which approach is generally BEST?

options.text: Allowlist validation — accept only known-good input matching the expected format
options.rationale: Allowlisting is more robust than blocklisting because it accepts only explicitly valid input, closing gaps attackers exploit in blocklists.

options.text: Blocklist a few known-bad characters and accept everything else
options.rationale: Blocklists routinely miss novel malicious inputs; allowlisting is preferred.

options.text: Accept all input without any validation
options.rationale: Trusting all input is the root cause of injection vulnerabilities.

options.text: Validate input only on the client side
options.rationale: Client-side validation is bypassable; server-side validation is required.

stem: A developer implements a custom homemade encryption routine for sensitive data. What is the MOST appropriate guidance?

options.text: Replace it with a vetted, standard cryptographic library/algorithm
options.rationale: Custom cryptography is error-prone and likely weak; standardized, peer-reviewed algorithms should be used instead.

options.text: Keep the custom routine because obscurity makes it strong
options.rationale: Security through obscurity is not reliable; the custom routine likely has flaws.

options.text: Publish the custom algorithm to prove it is secure
options.rationale: Publishing a homemade cipher does not make it secure; vetted standards are preferred.

options.text: Encrypt twice with the same weak routine
options.rationale: Repeating a weak custom routine does not make it secure.

stem: The OWASP Top 10 is best described as which of the following?

options.text: A widely used list of the most critical web-application security risks
options.rationale: The OWASP Top 10 catalogs the most critical web-app risks and is a common secure-coding reference.

options.text: A list of the ten fastest programming languages
options.rationale: OWASP Top 10 is about security risks, not language speed.

options.text: A hardware benchmarking standard
options.rationale: It is a software-security list, not a hardware benchmark.

options.text: A backup rotation schedule
options.rationale: It has nothing to do with backups.

stem: When an authorization check encounters an unexpected error, how should secure code MOST appropriately behave?

options.text: Fail securely — deny access by default on error
options.rationale: Failing securely (deny by default) ensures errors do not accidentally grant access, a core secure-design principle.

options.text: Fail open — grant access so users are not inconvenienced
options.rationale: Failing open on an authorization error can grant unauthorized access, a serious flaw.

options.text: Crash the whole server to be safe
options.rationale: Crashing harms availability and is not the intended fail-secure behavior.

options.text: Log the user in as administrator
options.rationale: Escalating to admin on error is dangerous and wrong.

stem: An application connects to its database using an account with full administrative rights. What is the BEST secure-coding improvement?

options.text: Use a least-privilege database account limited to the operations the app needs
options.rationale: A least-privilege service account limits damage if the app or its credentials are compromised.

options.text: Give the app account even more privileges for flexibility
options.rationale: Excess privileges increase the blast radius of a compromise.

options.text: Share the admin account across all applications
options.rationale: Shared admin accounts destroy accountability and over-grant access.

options.text: Hard-code the admin password in the source
options.rationale: Hard-coded credentials are easily extracted and should be avoided.

stem: An app passes unsanitized user input directly into an operating-system shell command. This is MOST accurately which vulnerability class?

options.text: Command injection (a form of injection)
options.rationale: Passing untrusted input into a shell command lets attackers execute arbitrary commands — command injection, an injection-class flaw.

options.text: Cross-site scripting
options.rationale: XSS involves injecting scripts into web pages, not OS shell commands.

options.text: A backup misconfiguration
options.rationale: This concerns unsafe command execution, not backups.

options.text: A physical security flaw
options.rationale: Command injection is a software flaw, not physical.

stem: To reduce risk from misconfiguration, how should an application's default settings BEST be configured?

options.text: Secure by default — restrictive settings, features off unless explicitly needed
options.rationale: Secure defaults minimize exposure so that safe behavior does not depend on someone remembering to lock things down.

options.text: Everything enabled and open by default
options.rationale: Open defaults maximize attack surface and rely on manual hardening that is often skipped.

options.text: Debug mode on in production by default
options.rationale: Debug mode in production leaks sensitive information and should be off.

options.text: Default admin credentials left unchanged
options.rationale: Default credentials are a classic weakness and must be changed.

stem: What is the MOST fundamental root cause of injection vulnerabilities?

options.text: Untrusted input being interpreted as code/commands rather than treated as data
options.rationale: Injection occurs when input crosses into the code/command context; keeping data separate from code (e.g., parameterization) prevents it.

options.text: Using too much memory
options.rationale: Memory usage is unrelated to injection root cause.

options.text: Slow network connections
options.rationale: Network speed does not cause injection.

options.text: Bright user-interface colors
options.rationale: UI colors have no relationship to injection.

stem: A user changes an 'id' parameter in a URL and views another user's private record. This flaw is MOST accurately which OWASP category?

options.text: Broken access control (insecure direct object reference)
options.rationale: Accessing another user's data by manipulating a reference without authorization checks is broken access control.

options.text: Cryptographic failure
options.rationale: The issue is missing authorization, not weak encryption.

options.text: A backup failure
options.rationale: This is an access-control flaw, not a backup problem.

options.text: A denial-of-service attack
options.rationale: No availability disruption is described; it is unauthorized data access.

stem: Parameterized queries (prepared statements) primarily defend against which vulnerability?

options.text: SQL injection
options.rationale: Prepared statements separate query structure from data, preventing SQL injection.

options.text: Physical theft of servers
options.rationale: Parameterized queries are a code defense, unrelated to physical theft.

options.text: Power outages
options.rationale: They have no bearing on power availability.

options.text: Wi-Fi eavesdropping
options.rationale: They protect against injection, not wireless interception.

stem: An app transmits passwords over plain HTTP and stores them unhashed. This MOST directly represents which OWASP category?

options.text: Cryptographic failures (sensitive data inadequately protected)
options.rationale: Failing to encrypt data in transit and to hash stored passwords is a cryptographic-failures issue.

options.text: A logging failure
options.rationale: The problem is missing encryption/hashing, not logging.

options.text: A fire-suppression failure
options.rationale: This is a software cryptography issue, not physical.

options.text: A UI design flaw
options.rationale: The flaw is inadequate protection of sensitive data, not UI design.

stem: Cross-site scripting (XSS) is MOST accurately categorized as which broader class of vulnerability?

options.text: Injection
options.rationale: XSS is an injection flaw where untrusted input is injected as script into web pages viewed by others.

options.text: Physical security
options.rationale: XSS is a software injection issue, not physical.

options.text: Backup mismanagement
options.rationale: XSS is unrelated to backups.

options.text: Power management
options.rationale: XSS has nothing to do with power.

stem: A secure-coding review finds credentials embedded directly in the source. What is the BEST remediation?

options.text: Remove the secrets from source and load them from a secrets vault at runtime
options.rationale: Secrets should be stored in a vault and injected at runtime, never hard-coded where anyone with code access can read them.

options.text: Leave them in the code but add a comment saying 'secret'
options.rationale: A comment does not protect the exposed credential.

options.text: Encode the secret in Base64 in the source
options.rationale: Base64 is trivially reversible and provides no protection.

options.text: Publish the secret in the documentation
options.rationale: Publishing the secret worsens the exposure.

stem: An application uses an outdated library with known critical vulnerabilities. Which secure-coding practice BEST addresses this OWASP category?

options.text: Keep dependencies patched and monitor them with SCA/SBOM
options.rationale: Tracking and updating components via SCA/SBOM addresses the 'vulnerable and outdated components' risk.

options.text: Ignore the library since it still runs
options.rationale: Running does not mean secure; known-vulnerable components must be updated.

options.text: Remove all logging around the library
options.rationale: Reducing logging hides problems and does not patch the component.

options.text: Assume the library is safe because it is popular
options.rationale: Popularity does not eliminate known vulnerabilities.

stem: An app checks a user's authorization only at login and then trusts them for the whole session, even as they access new resources. Which secure-design principle is MOST violated?

options.text: Complete mediation — every access should be authorized, not just the first
options.rationale: Complete mediation requires checking authorization on each access; trusting a single initial check enables privilege abuse.

options.text: Fail-open design is being followed correctly
options.rationale: This is a violation, not correct design; and fail-open is itself undesirable.

options.text: Least privilege is being maximized
options.rationale: The scenario is about repeated authorization checks, not privilege minimization, and it represents a violation.

options.text: Defense in depth is fully applied
options.rationale: Relying on one check is the opposite of layered mediation.

stem: An application records no security-relevant events, so intrusions go unnoticed. This MOST directly maps to which OWASP category?

options.text: Security logging and monitoring failures
options.rationale: Lack of security logging/monitoring prevents timely detection and response, a distinct OWASP risk category.

options.text: SQL injection
options.rationale: The issue is missing logging, not query injection.

options.text: Cryptographic failure
options.rationale: The issue is detection capability, not encryption.

options.text: A physical fire hazard
options.rationale: This is a software logging issue, not physical safety.

stem: Which practice is LEAST relevant to secure coding?

options.text: Choosing a visually pleasing variable-naming color in the editor
options.rationale: Editor color themes for variable names have no bearing on code security, making it least relevant.

options.text: Validating and sanitizing all input
options.rationale: Input validation is fundamental to secure coding.

options.text: Using parameterized queries
options.rationale: Parameterized queries prevent SQL injection, a core practice.

options.text: Enforcing authorization server-side
options.rationale: Server-side authorization is essential to prevent broken access control.
